#9637. Engineering a Secure Execution Environment for AI-Generated Artifacts

Software Engineer/TeamLead @ JetRockets | Ruby, Rails, PostgreSQL, Open Source contributor

Software Engineer/TeamLead @ JetRockets | Ruby, Rails, PostgreSQL, Open Source contributor

Software Engineer/TeamLead @ JetRockets | Ruby, Rails, PostgreSQL, Open Source contributor

In September I wrote about three security boundaries for hosting untrusted, AI-generated HTML. That one was about the browser. A page nobody reviewed runs in the browser of someone who is signed in to our platform, and the work was making sure it can't act as them. At the end I said the part where our assistant writes those pages on its own hadn't shipped yet.

It does now. And a month later it went one step further: the agent writes programs, and we run them on our own servers. This is how we set that up, how we check it, and what it cost us.

People kept taking what our assistant produced and hand-formatting it into slides. So we let the assistant build an editable PowerPoint deck from a chat, on the client's brand, and change it when asked.

The spec proposed a fixed library of slide layouts: the model fills a JSON structure, our code turns it into slides. It's the safe option, since nothing the model writes ever runs. We went the other way. The model writes a Node.js script against pptxgenjs, and the script builds the .pptx. What people ask for isn't a fixed set of deck types, and a script can compose whatever the content needs, with real text boxes, tables and native charts that stay editable in PowerPoint.

The price is obvious. Code a model wrote has to run somewhere. And the model doesn't write it from nothing: it reads the chat, the client's uploaded documents, search results from the web. Any of those can carry instructions. So the script is untrusted in the same way the HTML was, and for the same reason. We don't know who effectively wrote it.

There was a second reason for running code, and in the end it mattered more than decks. A model that writes slides blind produces text running off the edge and boxes stacked on top of each other. So every build comes back with a picture of each slide, the model looks, fixes what it sees, and builds again. Normally nothing is saved until it says the slides are clean. If time runs out, the last deck that built is kept, and the assistant says its last fixes weren't checked. Once that worked for decks, we did the same for HTML pages: every page the agent writes is opened in headless Chromium at a phone's width (up to three times a run), and the model gets pictures of it and the errors from its scripts. More on what that changed below.

All three model vendors we use offer some form of this: code the model writes runs in their environment. It would have been the fastest route, and we said no to it early. Two of the three run Python only, and our deck library is Node, but that wasn't the main reason.

Our product runs its AI work on chains of models from three vendors, with a fallback from one to the next. A feature built on one vendor's container works only on that vendor, and goes down with it. We had already decided that every AI feature has to work on all three. There is also the content itself: a deck is built from a client's strategy documents, and we didn't want those executing in a third party's environment.

The brand is the other half of that. A branded deck needs the brand's files: logos, and fonts the client has a license for. In a vendor's container those files would have to be uploaded next to the script before it could use them. In ours the model never gets them. It gets a list of what it may use, each file named by a reference like asset://bm_7f3a with its size and a note on where the brand uses it, and it writes that reference into the script or the page. Our app swaps the reference for the real file only on the way into the sandbox, so the files themselves go from our storage to our container and nowhere else. The provider does see the slides when the model looks at them, logo included, and that is the point of looking. What it sees is a picture of the slide, not the vector logo or the font files behind it.

So the execution environment is ours, and any model that can call a tool can drive it. The tool sends the script, our service runs it, and the pictures come back in the tool result. RubyLLM passes them the way each provider accepts them, inside the result for Claude and Gemini, as a user message right after it for OpenAI. The tools don't know any of that.

In the HTML article the target was the reader's session. Here there is no session in the room, and the list is different:

The sandbox is a small HTTP service of its own, built from a Debian image with Node 22, LibreOffice, Poppler and Chromium. It has two working endpoints and a health check. One takes a script and the brand kit's files and answers with the .pptx, a picture of every slide and each slide's text, or with what stopped it. The other takes an HTML page and answers with pictures of it top to bottom and a list of problems.

What it doesn't have matters more than what it does. No credentials, no database, no state between runs, no published port, no route from the public proxy. We deploy it with Kamal as an accessory next to the job workers, and the app reaches it over Docker's network by container name. If a script got full control of the service, it would find nothing worth stealing in it.

The container starts as root, and the first thing it does is close the door:

Loopback stays open, and so do the replies to connections that came in, since that's how the app gets its answer. Everything else is dropped. The last line is easy to miss: Docker's DNS resolver lives on a loopback address inside the container, so without it a script could still resolve names, and DNS is a channel on its own. Loopback has one more rule on top: the job's user is refused on the service's own port, so a script can't send requests to the service that is running it. Inbound works the same way in reverse: new connections reach only the service's port, so a port a job opens while it runs can't be reached from anything next to the container.

The same rules are set for IPv6. If the container isn't allowed to set its firewall, it refuses to start. A sandbox that comes up without its firewall looks exactly like one that has it, so we'd rather it didn't come up.

Pages get the same treatment inside the browser. Every request Chromium makes is answered by the sandbox itself, with the brand files the page was given, or refused. Windows the page opens and forms it submits go nowhere either, and WebRTC, which opens UDP sockets of its own, is kept behind the same dead end. An alert or print dialog is dismissed, so a page can't hold the line by waiting for a click.

The server stays root, because it has to keep the firewall and kill whatever a job leaves behind. The job doesn't. Each script, the check of the file it wrote, LibreOffice and the Poppler tools all run as a separate unprivileged user that has no capabilities and can't gain any.

Every capability is there for one reason: NET_ADMIN for the firewall at start, SETUID and SETGID to start a job as the job user, KILL to stop that user's processes, the last three so the server can hand a job its directory and then read and delete what it wrote. The filesystem is read-only apart from two tmpfs mounts: 1 GB for runs and 256 MB for /tmp. The script sees six environment variables and nothing else.

Runs go one at a time. After every step of a job (the script, the check, LibreOffice, the browser) the server kills every process the job user owns. When the run ends, it also deletes the run's directory, empties /tmp, /dev/shm and /dev/mqueue, and removes the user's System V IPC objects. A script that forks a process into the background and exits gets that process killed along with everything else.

The server never trusts what the script left. It reads the output with O_NOFOLLOW and only if it's a regular file, so a deck.pptx that is a symlink to something else is refused, not read. Unpacking and checking the archive happens as the job user too, never in the server's own process. There are limits on everything: 60 seconds for the script, 20 MB for the deck, 30 slides, 40 MB for all the pictures of one deck together. LibreOffice renders in a directory created after the script is dead, from bytes the server holds, so the script can't plant a profile or a font for it.

A sandbox is usually described by what it keeps in. The file it hands back deserves the same attention, because a third person opens it later, on their own machine.

A .pptx is a zip of XML files, and a relationship inside it can point outside the file. PowerPoint fetches such targets when the deck opens: a picture by URL tells its host who opened the deck and when, and a picture on a network share can make the reader's machine try to sign in to that share. So the check refuses any deck that points outside itself, except a web or mail hyperlink the reader chooses to click. The check also refuses anything in the file that runs code: OLE objects, packaged files, ActiveX controls, macros. A native chart keeps its own spreadsheet inside the deck, and that one is allowed. A file that holds the same part twice is refused outright, because one program may read the first copy and another the last, and so is a file with anything before or after the archive. When the brand fonts are put inside the deck after the check, the result is checked again. A page follows the same rule from the other side: it loads nothing from outside.

A few smaller rules came from the same way of looking at it. Sizes are capped and counted as the answer is read, so one build can't make the app hold hundreds of megabytes. A build whose caller hung up is stopped at once instead of keeping the line busy. A caller takes a place in the queue before its request body is read, and when the 8 places are taken, the next one is turned away. And the log line of a run says how many problems it had, never what they said, because a problem can quote the script, and the script can quote the client.

The service has an ordinary test suite that runs on a developer's machine. That suite can't test the sandbox itself: outside the container there is no firewall, no switch to the job user, no cleanup between runs as root.

So the same suite has a second mode. It builds the image, runs it with the production flags next to a neighbouring container, and checks from inside a job that it has no privileges and an environment of six names, can't reach the neighbour over TCP, UDP or IPv6, can't resolve names, can't reach the service's own port, can't be reached on a port it opens, can't read the server's process or files, can write only where it should, and leaves nothing for the next run: no files, no processes, no listeners, no shared memory. A page and the windows it opens are checked the same way. The last check starts the container without the right to set its firewall and expects it to refuse. The CI workflow that publishes the sandbox image runs this mode first, on the same source, and pushes only if it passes. It's slow and needs Docker, so it runs where the image is built, not with the app's own tests.

Before writing this I ran it again, and then attacked a fresh container by hand on top of it: HTTPS and raw TCP to the internet, DNS through Docker's resolver and through a public one, a symlink in place of the deck, a script that never ends, a deck with a picture on a remote host and one on a network share, a malformed request to the service, eleven callers at once, a job listening for connections from next door, a page opening a WebRTC connection, decks with an OLE object, with macros, and with a part written twice. Every one ended the way it should: a timeout or a refusal, the endless script stopped at 60 seconds, every one of those decks refused at the check, the service still answering, nine callers in line and two turned away. Where a case wasn't covered yet, it got a fix and a test before this went out.

The security work was the cost. Here is what we got for it.

On the same request, a page written blind kept its risk table as a table, and on a phone the main column ran off the screen inside a scrolling box. No automatic check flags that, because technically nothing is wrong. The page the model had looked at was rebuilt as cards. For decks, the first real run (four slides, one chart, two builds) took about 80 seconds, and the second build was the model fixing what it saw in the first.

It isn't free. A change to a page used to take a few seconds and now takes about a minute, because every change is opened and looked at again, a one-line edit included. I had a quick path that skipped the look for small edits, and we took it out: what a change did is only known after you see it. A run gets at most three looks at a page, so a model can't spend its budget looking, and the budget itself went from 4 minutes to 7. Every picture stays in the model's context, so a long deck revised many times costs real tokens. The 30-slide ceiling is also a cost ceiling.

Inline scripts in a page are checked with node --check, which parses them without running them. Running them is what the browser in the sandbox is for.

Runs go one at a time. Two people asking for decks at once wait for each other, and the app gives a build 5 minutes before it calls the sandbox unavailable. For now that's fine. If people start waiting, the plan is several job users running in parallel.

Without the sandbox, nothing gets made. If it's down, the run fails and the assistant says in the chat that it couldn't build the artifact. We'd rather say so than save a page nobody looked at.

It's a hardened container, not a virtual machine. For code that holds no secrets and can reach nothing, that's the trade we chose, and we wrote down when we'd revisit it. When we do, there are two directions. gVisor runs the same container on a kernel of its own in user space, needs nothing new from the host, and costs little extra memory. Docker Sandboxes, which Docker built this year for coding agents, gives every run a microVM with its own kernel and a network that is closed by default. It needs KVM on the host, and a VM per run brings its own kernel and Docker daemon, so it would want a host of its own rather than a place next to the app. Either one would sit under the same service without changing what it does.

Before you pick a provider's hosted container, check whether the feature has to survive that provider being down. Ours did, and that settled it in a day.

Treat the script the way you'd treat an uploaded file, because it is one. The model wrote it after reading things you don't control.

Start from what the service holds, not from what it blocks. A sandbox with no credentials, no database and no state is one where a full escape into the service finds nothing. Then block the network, including the DNS resolver and IPv6, and make the service refuse to start when it can't.

Look at every output format as something a third person will open. The run is only half of it.

And run your isolation tests where the isolation is. A green suite that runs as a normal user outside the container tells you nothing about the firewall.

Three Security Boundaries for Hosting Untrusted, AI-Generated HTML

#9636. Swarms, Flocks, Gangs: How to build, train, and evaluate multi-agent systems

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate

This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

That's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we update when we're dealing with many agents?

In this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

We've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI announced that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

We'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

This creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:

A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:

The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

This means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

The main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

In this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

For every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

In TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

Our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

Over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

The team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

The team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:

That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

Notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

No agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each update collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:

With eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

The model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each update generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts quickly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:

The figures above describe our original 75-update experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

Sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

One TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each update uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

This shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

To run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-update 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

Once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

This first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

#9635. How to Measure Product Success Without a Historical Baseline

Recognized data engineering expert and thought leader with more than 16years of experience architecting large-scale enterprise data platform

Recognized data engineering expert and thought leader with more than 16years of experience architecting large-scale enterprise data platform

Recognized data engineering expert and thought leader with more than 16years of experience architecting large-scale enterprise data platform

A data model, a KPI taxonomy and a 90-day plan for the stretch when nobody can tell you what “normal” looks like.

Three weeks after launch, someone senior will ask, “Is it working?”

If your answer is a dashboard with forty tiles, you’ve lost the room. If your answer is “we don’t have a baseline yet,” you’ve lost it more politely.

Most of the time the problem isn’t the engineering. It’s the order of operations. Teams instrument everything, argue about definitions in week six, and then find out that the numbers they’ve been quoting can’t be rebuilt. I’d rather you skip that part.

The pattern is familiar to anyone who has launched a data product. It goes like this. A product ships on a Tuesday. The team has page views, sign-ups and a dashboard somebody built over a weekend. By week three an executive asks whether it’s working, and the honest answer is that nobody has agreed what “working” means. By week six two teams are quoting two different activation numbers, and both are calculated correctly from two different definitions. By week ten someone proposes rebuilding the pipeline and finds that the aggregates they kept can’t answer the new question, because the raw events were summarized away on day one.

Nothing in that story is dramatic. No outage, no villain. The measurement design was simply decided by default, and defaults are expensive. That’s the failure this article is meant to prevent.

Every number below comes from one worked example with made-up data: a self-service reorder feature in a mobile app. I’ll flag it each time so nobody mistakes it for a benchmark.

Before any KPI gets a name, write down the decisions the numbers have to support. Not “what can we measure.” What will someone do differently on Monday because of this number?

Errors and support contacts per 1,000 reorders

If a metric can’t be tied to a row in a table like this one, I don’t build it yet. That rule alone has killed more dashboard requests than any prioritization meeting.

With no baseline, you will redefine your metrics. I don’t mean you might. You will. So the data model has to make that cheap.

A minimal raw table (Spark SQL-style syntax; adapt it to your engine):

Metrics live in a separate layer that reads from it. Here is a 30-day repeat-reorder cohort, assuming duplicates were already removed on event_id:

Look at what’s missing: no target, no dashboard logic. When the definition changes, you change one view and rebuild from the log. That is the entire payoff of the raw layer.

One more query belongs next to it, and almost nobody writes it on day one. It tells you how much of each day’s data arrives late:

Most KPI lists fail because everything sits at the same level: revenue next to page load time next to a survey score. Nobody can say which number moves which. I use four tiers, and the fourth is the one teams skip.

The result the product exists to deliver

What must not get worse while you optimise

Completeness, late arrivals, duplicates

One outcome. Three or four drivers. A guardrail for every way you could “win” by breaking something else. If you can’t draw your KPIs as a tree like this, you have a list, not a taxonomy.

A pipeline problem that looks like a business trend is the most expensive kind of wrong.

That is why data health gets its own tier. In a new product, a dropped event or a late batch shows up as “customer behaviour changed,” and somebody builds a strategy on it.

Every KPI gets a card. One page, versioned, stored where people can find it. Here is one filled in:

Of customers who completed a first reorder, the share who completed another within 30 days

repeated ÷ activated, by weekly cohort (view: m_repeat_reorder_30d)

Internal test accounts; reorders later refunded in full

v1.0, 2026-11-10. Every change needs a dated entry

A cohort is incomplete until 30 days have passed

The version line matters more than it looks. A chart that quietly changes meaning is the fastest way I know to burn an executive’s trust.

Ownership matters as much as the fields. The named owner approves any change to a definition, and the change log records who asked and why. It sounds bureaucratic until the first time two dashboards disagree and you can settle it in five minutes instead of five meetings.

The caveats line earns its place too. A 30-day metric for a cohort that activated 10 days ago has only seen a third of its window. Report it as final and you will “discover” a retention problem that is really just arithmetic. Only publish a cohort once its window has closed.

“We have no baseline” is a starting condition, not a verdict. You manufacture one, deliberately, in three moves.

Observe first. Say out loud that weeks one to six are for learning. Report the numbers, set no targets, and label the dashboard “baseline in progress.” Early users are your most curious users, so the first weeks flatter you. In the worked example, activation opens at 31%, peaks at 36% in week two, and settles near 26% by week six.

Freeze it as a range. Pool weeks 7 to 12: 6,550 customers saw the feature and 1,692 completed a first reorder. That gives a baseline of 25.8%, with a 95% interval of 24.8% to 26.9%. Publish that, dated and versioned, and measure change against it from then on. One more number to hand your stakeholders: a single week of about 1,100 viewers carries roughly ±2.5 points of noise on its own. A week at 24% against a baseline of 25.8% is not a decline. It’s Tuesday.

Know how much data you need. For a rate near 26%, the sample for a 95% interval is about n = 1.96² × p × (1 − p) ÷ e². Half-width ±3 points needs roughly 820 customers. ±2 points needs about 1,850. ±1 point needs about 7,400. If your weekly volume is smaller than that, widen the window instead of pretending the weekly number means something.

The second trap is lateness. Here is week four, reported as the days after the week closed went by:

Somebody who screenshots the day-one number and puts it in a slide has just reported a drop that never happened. Two fixes. Show data-health metrics beside every KPI, and don’t publish a week until its late-arrival share has flattened. Then you don’t restate in public.

Borrow proxies, and label them. A similar feature, an industry figure or a pilot can give you a rough range before you have your own. Call it an assumption every time you show it.

Ship the event contract. Turn on the raw log and the data-health checks. Write the decision table.

Observe. Build the metric views. Write definition cards for the outcome and drivers.

KPIs labelled “baseline in progress”, no targets

Freeze the baseline as a range. Add guardrail thresholds. Version everything.

Review the taxonomy. Retire KPIs nobody used. Set the first targets.

Back to the executive in week three. You don’t have a baseline, but you can still give a useful answer. I use three sentences: what we know, how sure we are, and when we’ll know more.

“Activation over the last two weeks is 27.8%, give or take about 1.8 points. Early weeks run high because the people trying a new feature first are the keenest, so I expect it to settle nearer 26%. We’ll freeze a baseline at week seven and I’ll bring you a range then.”

That answer does something a bare number can’t. It says the figure is provisional, shows the uncertainty, predicts the direction of travel, and gives a date. (In the worked example those two weeks cover 2,450 customers who saw the feature, of whom 682 completed a first reorder.) Executives will forgive a number that moves if you told them it would. They won’t forgive one that moves without warning.

Decide before you measure. Store events, derive metrics. Tier your KPIs and give each one a card. Treat the first six weeks as baseline-building, then freeze a range and version it. Expect your first reads to be wrong and have a plan for restating them quietly.

A product with no baseline is uncomfortable. It’s also the only time you get to design the measurement properly from the start. Most teams only get that chance once.

How to Measure and Optimize AI Agent Workflow Costs

Recognized data engineering expert and thought leader with more than 16years of experience architecting large-scale enterprise data platform

#9634. Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

Parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

This latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry

We trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

The matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

NaViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

The built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 shows three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

Fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

Double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass

Figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

The worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

Figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

#9633. Introducing the llama.cpp benchmark dashboard for AMD Ryzen and Radeon

The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:

Both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

The model set evolves and currently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

The explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

Standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

Thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

#9632. Building Voice Agents with LiveKit and Anthropic Claude: A Practical Engineering Guide

A voice agent can produce accurate answers and still feel unusable. A delayed response, an interruption handled incorrectly, or a tool call that takes several seconds can make an otherwise intelligent assistant frustrating to talk to.

Building reliable voice agents requires more than connecting a language model to speech recognition. Developers need to coordinate audio streaming, conversational reasoning, turn detection, speech synthesis, and backend execution under strict latency constraints.

LiveKit and Anthropic Claude provide a practical architecture for tackling these problems. LiveKit handles real-time media and agent orchestration, while Claude provides contextual reasoning, language understanding, and tool-driven decision-making.

This guide explores how to combine them, where production systems commonly fail, and which engineering decisions have the greatest impact on performance.

The most practical approach to integrating Claude with LiveKit is a cascaded speech-to-text (STT), large language model (LLM), and text-to-speech (TTS) pipeline.

Each component has a distinct responsibility:

Consider an appointment-scheduling assistant.

A caller says, "Can you move my appointment to Friday afternoon?" LiveKit receives the audio, an STT provider transcribes the request, and Claude interprets the scheduling intent. The agent checks appointment availability through an authorized backend tool, confirms the proposed change, and generates a spoken response.

The important distinction is that Claude is the reasoning layer, not the audio transport or speech synthesis engine.

LiveKit's official Anthropic integration supports both Python and Node.js, allowing developers to use Claude within its agent session architecture.

Engineering takeaway: Keep transport, transcription, reasoning, synthesis, and business logic independently replaceable. This makes performance tuning and provider migration significantly easier.

Latency is one of the most important performance indicators in conversational AI.

A voice agent's response time is influenced by several stages:

Optimizing only the language model rarely solves the complete problem.

A user might say, "I need to change my delivery address..." and pause briefly before continuing.

A simple voice activity detector may interpret that silence as the end of the request. The agent begins responding before the user has finished.

LiveKit addresses this with configurable endpointing and multimodal turn detection.

According to the LiveKit turn detector documentation, standard endpointing defaults range from 0.5 to 3.0 seconds, while its multimodal turn detector reduces those defaults to 0.3 to 2.5 seconds.

These are configuration delays, not guaranteed end-to-end response times.

Start by measuring transcription completion, end-of-turn delay, LLM first-token latency, and TTS startup separately.

Use streaming Claude responses so speech synthesis can begin before the entire answer is generated. Anthropic supports incremental output through server-sent event streaming.

Also consider preemptive generation, which allows the agent to begin preparing a response before the user's turn is fully confirmed.

However, speculative execution can waste inference requests when users continue speaking.

Engineering takeaway: Optimize perceived response latency without sacrificing turn-taking accuracy. A slightly slower response that respects natural pauses is often preferable to an agent that repeatedly interrupts users.

Text-based assistants and voice agents require different response strategies.

A detailed, multi-paragraph answer might be useful in a chat interface but exhausting when read aloud.

Claude should therefore receive instructions designed specifically for conversational speech.

Effective voice-agent instructions establish a few clear constraints:

For example, when checking a refund, the agent should say, "I'll check the refund status," rather than "Your refund has been processed" before receiving confirmation.

LiveKit's Claude plugin documents Claude Sonnet as a supported default option and provides configurable parameters for response length, tool choice, and parallel tool execution.

For production environments, benchmark multiple Claude models using representative conversations rather than selecting one solely by its benchmark scores.

Measure response quality alongside time to first token, tool-use accuracy, token consumption, and cost per successful task.

A faster model may be suitable for routine questions, while more complex workflows may benefit from a model with stronger reasoning capabilities.

Anthropic's prompting guidance is useful when developing concise instructions and reliable tool behavior.

Engineering takeaway: Optimize Claude for the spoken interaction, not just textual correctness. Response length, clarification behavior, and confirmation policies directly affect the user experience.

A voice agent becomes operationally useful when it can retrieve information and execute authorized actions.

For example, a customer-support agent may need to:

Claude can select and structure tool requests, but the application backend should enforce authorization, validation, and execution rules.

Suppose a customer requests an address change.

Claude can identify the new address and determine that an update operation is needed. However, the backend should validate the user's permissions, verify the order's status, and reject updates that violate business rules.

For state-changing operations, use idempotency keys to prevent duplicate execution after retries or interrupted connections.

Keep tool responses compact. Returning an entire customer record when the agent only needs delivery status increases context size and creates unnecessary data exposure.

For teams implementing these patterns, agentic AI workflows and conversational AI architectures provide useful context for designing connected, action-oriented systems.

Anthropic's tool-use documentation explains how Claude interacts with external functions.

Engineering takeaway: Treat Claude as an intelligent decision-making component, not the ultimate authority over business operations.

Interruption handling is one of the clearest differences between a demo and a production-ready voice agent.

Imagine an agent explaining a payment issue when the customer interrupts: "Actually, I want to speak to someone."

The system should stop speaking, process the new request, and avoid continuing the abandoned explanation.

LiveKit supports interruption detection and configurable turn-handling behavior. Its adaptive interruption handling is designed to distinguish meaningful interruptions from background speech and conversational acknowledgements.

A common implementation mistake is treating generated text as if the user heard all of it.

If TTS is interrupted halfway through a response, the conversation state should reflect what was actually delivered, not simply what Claude generated.

Otherwise, subsequent reasoning may depend on information the user never heard.

Developers should distinguish between generated, queued, played, and interrupted speech whenever managing conversational state.

For longer sessions, summarize resolved context while preserving unfinished tasks, confirmed entities, and pending approvals.

Engineering takeaway: Conversation memory must represent the actual interaction, including interruptions and incomplete responses.

Voice agents have a different cost structure from traditional chatbots. Their operating expenses may include audio transport, transcription, LLM tokens, speech synthesis, telephony, and external service calls.

Long conversations can become particularly expensive when the same instructions and conversation history are repeatedly sent to the model.

Anthropic's prompt caching documentation describes cache-read pricing of 0.1 times the standard input-token price for many supported models, with model-specific exceptions.

For applications that reuse long system instructions or stable reference material, caching can reduce repeated input-processing costs.

Additional optimizations include limiting unnecessary context, minimizing verbose tool outputs, and avoiding full-response regeneration after interruptions.

LiveKit's agent dispatch documentation reports infrastructure designed to support hundreds of thousands of new connections per second, with typical dispatch times under 150 milliseconds. This describes its dispatch infrastructure, not the throughput guarantee of an individual application.

Actual capacity still depends on worker resources, speech providers, model rate limits, and concurrent tool execution.

The LiveKit dispatch documentation provides additional deployment details.

Engineering takeaway: Model concurrency, provider limits, and cost per completed interaction before increasing traffic. Infrastructure capacity alone does not determine application scalability.

A voice agent should be tested as a real-time system, not simply evaluated through text prompts.

Text-only evaluations miss audio quality, transcription errors, conversational overlap, and speech synthesis failures.

LiveKit exposes session metrics covering transcription delay, end-of-turn detection, LLM processing, and TTS startup.

Its session tracing documentation provides a framework for investigating where latency accumulates.

Testing should include noisy environments, different accents, long pauses, rapid corrections, overlapping speech, and unexpected requests.

LiveKit's agent simulation tools support audio-based testing that evaluates turn-taking failures and conversational behavior.

For sensitive workflows, add explicit authorization checks, audit trails, data-retention controls, and human escalation paths.

Engineering takeaway: A voice agent is production-ready only when its conversational quality, operational reliability, and failure behavior are measurable.

Building effective voice agents with LiveKit and Anthropic Claude is primarily an exercise in real-time systems engineering.

LiveKit provides the media transport and conversational orchestration needed to manage live audio. Claude provides the language understanding, reasoning, and tool-selection capabilities required for more complex interactions.

The most important design decisions concern the boundaries between those components.

Start with a narrow workflow, establish a measurable latency budget, verify tool execution independently, and test interruptions under realistic audio conditions.

A successful voice agent is not simply one that can speak naturally. It is one that listens correctly, responds at the right moment, executes actions safely, and recovers predictably when something goes wrong.

#9631. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

Tel Aviv, Israel, November 26th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--ApexFlow, a mobile advertising technology company, today announced the launch of Nuvvo, a new supply intelligence and monetization offering designed to bring greater precision to mobile advertising. Nuvvo connects an established publisher network with advanced decisioning technology, helping programmatic buyers discover relevant in-app opportunities while enabling developers to grow advertising revenue.

ApexFlow's technology is shaped by its experience operating two acquired app studios and a portfolio of over 100 mobile apps across education, travel and gaming, with more than 100 million cumulative downloads. That firsthand perspective informs how the company evaluates inventory quality, user engagement and monetization performance.

Nuvvo brings together contextual, audience and performance signals with AI-driven yield optimization, dynamic pricing and demand routing. These capabilities inform inventory selection by app category, market and ad format, turning a broad range of mobile impressions into more focused, curated buying opportunities.

Nuvvo builds on a broad and growing network of direct app developer and publisher relationships. Partners receive hands-on support from ApexFlow's monetization team, access to programmatic demand and opportunities to connect with direct campaigns, including through the company's recent collaboration with Catch New York, a New York-based advertising agency.

ApexFlow's internal analysis indicates monthly U.S. audience reach exceeding 200 million users. Nuvvo pairs this scale with signal-informed selection to help buyers identify inventory aligned with campaign needs. Supply is available through open auctions and private marketplaces (PMPs), supporting supply-path visibility.

"Scale creates opportunity, but intelligence creates value," said Moshe Cohen, CEO of ApexFlow. "Nuvvo brings together direct supply relationships, meaningful signals and real-time decisioning so buyers can find the inventory that matters and publishers can unlock more value from every opportunity."

Programmatic buyers interested in Nuvvo supply, and app developers interested in joining the program, can contact team@apexflowsdk.com. Learn more at apexflowsdk.com/nuvvo.

ApexFlow is a mobile advertising technology company focused on AI-driven monetization, direct publisher partnerships and intelligent mobile supply curation. Its technology helps app developers optimize advertising revenue while connecting programmatic buyers with relevant in-app inventory.

#9627. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

Cover photo by Danielle Sykes; food styling by Kaitlin Wayne.

#9626. Google Search Console for beginners: 4 reports worth checking every week

If you run a website and have never opened Google Search Console, you are flying blind. The tool is free, and it is the only place that shows how Google actually sees your site: which pages are indexed, which queries bring impressions, and how many people clicked.

Start by verifying ownership at search.google.com/search-console. You can prove it with an HTML file, a meta tag in your site header, or a DNS record. Data only starts collecting after verification, and it does not backfill the period before.

This is the most useful one. It shows clicks, impressions, click-through rate (CTR) and average position. The practical read: a page with many impressions but few clicks is shown by Google, but its title and description do not persuade people to click. That is usually the easiest win on a small site. Filter by query, page or country to dig in.

It lists which pages are indexed and which are not, with a reason. Not every reason is a problem. Google itself says some exclusions are normal, such as pages you redirected on purpose or alternate pages with correct tags. Review the reasons before you worry.

It tells you the status of one specific page: indexed or not, when Google last crawled it, and whether it has mobile usability issues. After publishing a new post you can request indexing here. The request does not guarantee speed or ranking.

Submit your sitemap here. If you use Rank Math or Yoast, you already have one. It helps Google discover your pages in an organized way, especially on a new site.

Four reports are enough to watch the health of a site in Google Search: Performance, Page indexing, URL Inspection and Sitemaps. Verify your site today and make the weekly check a habit.

I wrote this guide first in Arabic for small-business owners. The Arabic version is here: smarter-set.com/google-search-console-guide
