#9520. 13 Sam's Club Bakery Items, Ranked Worst To Best

Sam's Club bakery solves the puzzle of how to get great baked goods at exceptional prices without having to hunt down a standalone bakery. The full-service department offers everything from sliced bread and rolls for everyday use to custom cakes for your most special occasions. Like the other items under the warehouse roof, the bakery stocks bulk quantities and super-sized versions of many of its best-loved bakes, giving your bank account a bit of a breather without requiring you to give up your appetite for the good stuff.

To get the best of the Sam's Club bakery, you'll want to know which picks are worth your money and which you can keep rolling right on past. I scooped up a selection of breads, rolls, and sugary delights to put under the microscope — my taste buds — and see how they rank amongst one another. Simple items like plain bagels shared the table with deluxe creations like caramel pecan banana loaf, all purchased at my Phoenix, Arizona-area Sam's locations. Prices and products shown are likely to vary based on region and warehouse. Clearly, membership has its privileges, but they're not all equally worth your money or your attention.

The double-baguette bag at Sam's Club was a qualified bargain at $2.98 at the time of purchase, though the bread inside is skinnier than a regular loaf. It's crusty and tender, perfect for breaking off chunks and dipping into olive oil or cheese dip. But it does limit your uses to silver dollar-sized slices, making mini garlic toast or bruschetta the most likely purposes. Slicing it lengthwise in longer sections will extend your toasting potential, but it's still a lot of bread to blow through before it starts to get even crustier on the counter.

Unless you have a house load of diners to feed, you may be getting more bread than you need, in a size and shape that makes using leftovers a bit limited. So while the bread itself is a wonderful version of a bakery-style baguette, the drawbacks of having two super-skinny loaves to work through may be reason enough to make a more suitable choice than this grocery store French bread.

There's no sense in raving over how good a plain bagel can be. They're plain for a reason: so they can hold all kinds of spreads and shmears and fillings without the taste of ramped-up bread getting in the way. But that doesn't mean every bakery gets the basic formula for plain bagels right. So having a bodacious bag of six overly large, unadorned bagels waiting at Sam's Club, among the fancier flavors, is a comfort to the purists of the bread-loving world. They do make an attractive haul at only $3.82 for six large pre-cut bagels, so there's that, at least.

I'm a fan of bagels, largely for the dense chewiness they offer, similar to a pretzel but with more potential for add-ons that don't fall off. I'd love to endorse these bagels more heartily, since they do their job perfectly well at a price that doesn't feel like you're being gouged. But in the end, they're just bagels, and Sam's has so many preferable baked goods waiting to be tossed in your cart.

Sam's Club is famous for its generous 12-inch pumpkin pies that appear at holiday time, priced at a seasonally considerate $5.98. But beyond the size and price, the warehouse bakery doesn't do much out of the ordinary with this bake. The crust is standard, the filling is customary, and the experience of digging into a slice is perfectly passable. In fact, if you're a dessert traditionalist, this will do nicely to replace anything you were planning on making yourself.

But the fact that the company mass-produces its pumpkin pies every year means you know exactly what you're getting here. If you keep your expectations in check and top it with a drizzle of chocolate or caramel sauce, plus some king-sized dollops of whipped cream, you can make it through another serving this year. Just don't count on it being anything more than average, even under all the decorations. You might even fare a little better with the comparable-yet-superior Costco pumpkin pie this year instead.

Something about the recipe Sam's Club bakery uses for its yeast dinner rolls makes them better than the thaw-and-bake versions I've become accustomed to. The chewy crust and soft centers of these baked spheres make them far too easy to snack on, which could readily deplete your stock for actual meals. The oversized bag comes with 24 rolls, so maybe you'll have enough for both if you can keep your appetite for bread snacks under control.

Maybe the best thing about these rolls is the price. You can drop $3.98 and end up with more bread than you can shake a stick at — a true magic trick in an economy that seems intent on crushing shoppers just hoping to come home with the basics. It'll put your imagination to the test when you realize your leftovers are crying out for creativity — cream puffs, mini-sandwiches, and bread pudding are all possibilities. Even if you freeze what you don't use for meals down the line, you'll be glad you made the purchase.

Similar to the yeast dinner rolls, Sam's Club bakery's brioche slider rolls are three-bite beauties that come pre-sliced to be filled with your favorite accouterments. But whether you opt to use them as dinner rolls or just toast them up and spread a little peanut butter inside instead of making actual sliders, they'll be just as satisfying. They have a buttery, eggy flavor that mimics full-sized brioche buns; the only thing reduced here is the scale, and even that makes them a fun choice for kid-size sandwiches of all sorts.

For $6.98, you get a generous stash of 24 slider buns. That may seem like too many, but if you use them in place of sliced bread for school lunches and work them into weekend meals, you'll blow through a whole bag before you know it. And if they're among your DIY barbecue spread or holiday celebration as cold cut holders, your guests are sure to gush over how cute and delicious they are.

Tangy, chewy, and ready to eat right out of the bag, the sliced sourdough loaves from Sam's Club bakery are a fantastic alternative to the rectangular bagged loaves the warehouse sells in its commercial bread aisle. It's the sort of sturdy bread that holds up well as grilled cheese sandwiches, Reubens without rye, and French toast, though you'll need to cut the slices in half for easier handling. And you can certainly cut it into strips to add to your grazing board for get-togethers or brunch sessions. It's the every-bread, and it's only $3.96 a loaf.

I tried to think of some drawbacks for this accommodating bake, but came up short. Despite having a host of sugary bites on the list that knocked my socks off, I thought this sourdough was excellent. It's pushed aside my usual go-to seedy whole-grain loaves to become my preferred full-size bread and an every-visit purchase.

Cocktail croissants, as Sam's Club calls them, are the bakery's sensibly sized version of the French classic, given all the love and attention of their continental counterparts, even in a warehouse grocery department setting. There's flakiness galore, thanks to an all-butter recipe that also comes through in the rich flavor. A carton of 20 croissants priced at $5.98, yet made with the same quality as their boulangerie counterparts, could be the bargain of our lifetimes.

The size is perfect for snacking, much better than the larger, sandwich-friendly croissants that cry out for fillings. Sure, you can break a bigger croissant into smaller pieces to make noshing a little more restrained. But when you can complete one in a few bites and walk away? That's sensibly sized croissant business. And if you're a fan of French pastries but cringe at spending big money to enjoy them, this first-rate batch of happiness is your golden opportunity, no splurging necessary.

Now this savage bake looks like the Ferrari of Sam's Club offerings, even before you take it out of the box. Through the cellophane window on top, you can see a heart-stopping coating of crumble in the perfect shade of toasted brown. The split in the top reveals a peek of golden pound cake. The overall effect is that you've stumbled onto the most gourmet banana bread you've ever encountered — right across from the bulk fabric softener and double-paned window vendors.

The chewy crust is just shy of decadence, feeling more like an old-fashioned homemade crumble top without the oats. The banana bread beneath is equal parts sweet loaf and pound cake, capturing the cozy vibe but with a stroke of elegance that elevates it. I would eat this in all forms: cold out of the freezer, room temperature straight out of the box, or warmed up with a scoop of ice cream on the side. There's no situation that this fantastic loaf can't handle.

Gourmet bakeries have nothing on the patisserie spirit of Sam's Club mini creme pies. These refrigerated bakes shrink the lush goodness of full-sized pies into a six-pack of petite pastries, two each of chocolate creme, peanut butter chocolate, and cherry cheese pie. The reduced scale doesn't diminish the delicious returns; there's bold flavor and silky texture that make even a single slice a luxurious moment.

Though all of these pies are a real treat, there's a definite hierarchy to their enjoyability. The cherry cheese pie is a mellow bite that resurrects the vintage pie flavor from long-ago Sunday dinner desserts, while the chocolate creme reminds me of a dessert-style specialty. But the top spot belongs to the peanut butter chocolate pie, which calls to mind luxury cheesecakes made by maestros of the baking world. It's a sweet dream of a Sam's Club baked goodie, and at $10.98 for six, it's one that doesn't require reservations — of any kind.

Any Sam's Club shopper will tell you that the bakery muffins are a cake situation, not a muffin scenario. These super-sweet, super-sized bakes are too big and too delicious to qualify as traditional muffins, and when the warehouse puts a holiday spin on the usual recipes, that dessert-ready razzmatazz doubles up. They're the domed bakery-style muffins too, so they look extra grand on your snacking spread.

I've had the store's traditional chocolate, blueberry, and banana nut muffins enough to be inured to their charms by now. But slicing into these three upgraded flavors was a seasonal revelation I won't soon get over. The red velvet is the best of the bunch, tasting like a pricey chef-inspired creation, while the pumpkin spice takes a more measured approach than the usual fall-flavored treats. And the butter pecan is a study in subtlety, with just the right balance of sweet and earthy notes. These should be year-round items.

Another refrigerated item due to the meltable toppings and delicate frosting, the gourmet cupcake eight-pack at Sam's Club bakery is a fancier take on the workaday cupcakes that come in a set of 30, and all taste exactly the same. In this package, you get a variety of chocolate, strawberry, and Meyer lemon, all wearing the frills and finery you'd find in a much pricier cupcake at a specialty shop. The $12.97 price tag that splits into $1.62 per cake assures you that you can have nice things without having to cash in your IRA.

Even if you choose to crack open your piggy bank for these, you'll be getting more than your money's worth. The chocolate cupcake is exceptional, lush, and over-packed with fudgy goodness thanks to a generous heap of ganache frosting. The strawberry is well-balanced, with its own floral ganache whip, and the Meyer lemon, with a dollop of gelee in the center, is bright as sunshine, authentic-tasting. There's a moist crumb and silky frosting in every cake, too. They're a little too complex to pass off as a home bake, but these are top-tier bakes that make a perfect meal finisher at a dinner party or a lovely surprise for birthday revelers.

I'm a frequent Sam's Club shopper, so I had some idea of which items I thought would be worth including. But with items changing so often and seasonal picks popping up throughout the year, I also grabbed some new selections to give my list a bit of variety. Even familiar items like bagels and baguettes took on a different status when compared to novelties like specialty banana bread and gourmet brownies.

To taste test everything fairly, I used my standard method: the one-bite sample. I gauged freshness and texture as well as taste to arrive at an all-encompassing enjoyability factor for each item. Anything that was deemed worthy of a second or third bite became an obvious high-ranking find, while the items that were less captivating sank to the bottom. The standard-issue picks that were neither dazzling nor disappointing fell somewhere in the middle of the list.

#9519. The Elephant in the Rheum – “Burnout” Among the Workforce

Feelings of stress, fatigue, and exhaustion – what is being described as “burnout” – have become a common occurrence among providers, including rheumatologists, with important implications in clinical practice. Various surveys and studies have reported a substantial prevalence of burnout (approximately 50%) among rheumatology providers.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (UNC), joins us on this episode to provide deeper insight on the issue of “burnout” from a clinical practice standpoint.

Read the full transcript of the episode here.

Beth L. Jonas, MD, is the Reeves Foundation Distinguished Professor of Medicine and chief of the Division of Rheumatology, Allergy, and Immunology at UNC.

A recipient of a 2015 Rheumatology Research Foundation (RRF) Clinician Scholar Educator Award, Dr Jonas has developed a novel curriculum in Rheumatology in the Foundation Phase at UNC. She is a clinician educator and has an active rheumatology practice, where she sees patients with a wide spectrum of inflammatory rheumatic disorders. She teaches rheumatology to medical students, residents, and fellows and is actively involved in curricular development to train both physicians and advance practice providers in rheumatology.

Dr Jonas currently serves on the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Workforce Solutions Committee. She has previously served as the chair of the ACR Committee on Training and Workforce and has served as co-chair of the ACR In-Training Examination Taskforce. She has served on the board of the Rheumatology Research Foundation as well as the RRF Scientific Advisory Committee.

Dr Jonas is a founding member of the Carolinas Fellows Collaborative (CFC), a group of program directors from the Carolinas who work to enhance the education of their collective trainees. Dr Jonas was honored as the ACR Distinguished Rheumatology Program Director in 2015.

#9517. The two-second step to caramelize your pie crust : Just add sugar.

Most pie recipes will instruct you to sprinkle sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar on top of your egg-washed pie crust just before baking, so the coarse sugar can make those edges extra-crunchy and add a bit of glittery sheen. But why stop there — what if the bottom crust got the same treatment too?

That's what our Test Kitchen wondered while developing a new galette recipe for our newest cookbook (coming out next year!). While working on an apricot galette recipe, they tried adding a finishing sugar to the bottom of the dough before baking, and found that it created a crunchy, sugary, caramelized crust that elevated the entire dessert.

As an added bonus, this technique can help ensure a crunchy, well-browned bottom crust;  consider this step another line of defense against a soggy bottom, like baking your pie on a pizza stone or steel or baking pie on the bottom rack of the oven,

You can apply it to any pie (or galette!) recipe while rolling out the dough. Here’s how to do it:

On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough to a 10" to 12" round (aim for the smaller diameter for pie crusts, and larger for galettes). Sprinkle around 1 tablespoon of sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar all over the dough. (It’s important to only use these larger, coarse-grained sugars — we don’t recommend using granulated sugar.) Sprinkle lightly with flour, then continue to roll the dough to reach a 12" to 14" round. Carefully invert the dough round so that the sugared side is on the bottom of the pie pan (to make a single or double crust pie) or parchment paper (to make a galette).

Use this step in classic applications like apple pie where sparkling sugar can cover the entire thing, from top to bottom crust. Or, use it in custard pies like pecan or pumpkin. If you’re going the galette route for Thanksgiving, use it in our Apple Butter Apple Galette or Tiny Apple Tarts for Two. Regardless of the pie you choose, the crust — not the filling! — may be what steals the show.

#9510. 8 of our employee-owners’ favorite family recipes for the holidays  : Celebrate the season with us.

The holidays are always a big deal here at King Arthur, and this year we’re celebrating with something extra-special: our brand-new Enjoy the Bake campaign, which is all about the joy of baking together.

Enjoy the Bake is a reminder that memories are made around a mixing bowl, and traditions are passed down in the kitchen. In honor of this precious holiday baking season, our employee-owners are sharing the family-favorite recipes that mean the most to them this time of year.

“Every year since I was in grade school, my mom and I would spend the night before Thanksgiving making every type of pie that the family wants. We were a family of six, and everyone's taste was different. What makes it such a lasting memory is how much of a well-oiled machine my mom and I were when working together in the kitchen. She would make pie crust, and I would make all the fillings! Years later, we still make pies for the holidays — but in our own homes — and then come together for the holiday.”

Martina Fleurrey, Customer Experience Supervisor

Get the recipes: Apple Pie, Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie, and Pumpkin Pie

“I grew up with my grandparents making giant batches of pizzelle for the holidays. Their delicate crunch and subtle hint of vanilla are things I'll always associate with the season. My dad now has the pizzelle press, and every holiday, we carry on the tradition, taking turns pouring the batter, pressing, and carefully removing each one.”

“My mom and I entered a gingerbread house contest every year, and making that together was so fun, as was shopping for the candy. More than once, our design was completely themed around a weird gummy shape we couldn't say no to. It was an opportunity to bake gingerbread in increasingly odd shapes, get creative with themes and ingredients, and channel our cheeky humor.” (Learn how to make your own gingerbread house in our new On-Demand Class: Gingerbread House Baking, Building & Decorating.)

Annabelle Shippee, Social Media Strategist

Get the recipe: Construction Gingerbread for Gingerbread Houses

“Each year on Thanksgiving my paternal grandmother, who had 10 kids, would make pies and bring them to each of her local kids. One year, she made two for us, as we were having a big gathering and pumpkin is my dad's favorite pie — one pie was for the gathering and one for just our family. My dad put his personal pumpkin pie upstairs in the closet. About a month later, I hear a screech and come running: My mom found the pie … which was now all moldy. We still laugh about that to this day. The last couple of years, I've been making our Pumpkin Cheesecake Pie as a new elevated version of my grandmother's classic pumpkin pie. It's been a fan favorite, and it's so beautiful to slice.”

Jordan Kilby, Director, Digital Marketing and Customer Data

“One of our family traditions is sausage bread on Christmas Eve. It's served as an appetizer (but to be honest, we all eat enough of it to be a full meal). This is one of my favorite family recipes, not only because it's delicious, but it's also nostalgic. My grandmother made it every year, and my Aunt Millie included it as one of the recipes to pass down in a family cookbook she created. My brother and I have baked it for many years, and now my kids are starting to take over the baking. (We are all still doing the eating.) It's so good that everyone looks forward to it — probably the reason it's lasted four generations.”

Get the recipe: The dough is similar to this Braided Stromboli recipe, using Italian sausage, parsley, and Romano cheese as the filling

“We started having Cranberry Orange Scones on Christmas morning back when I was a little kid. We'd use the King Arthur scone mix and the special scone pan; I loved pressing the dough into the wedge-shaped wells. At one point, we decided that we'd use orange juice as the liquid in the dough instead of milk for extra orange flavor, and that became our ‘secret trick’ that made the scones so delicious. Nowadays, we make the recipe from scratch (even though I still love the box mix) and have scones and coffee while we open stockings on Christmas morning. They're the perfect treat for our family — they feel special without being fussy, so we're able to mix them up and bake them fresh without taking away from our family time.”

“My mom has a late fall birthday, and since childhood she has insisted that instead of a cake she get a pumpkin pie to celebrate. So over the years, in the weeks between her birthday and Thanksgiving, my family ate a lot of pumpkin pie in all varieties: store-bought, homemade, topped with pecans and whipped cream, graham cracker crust and flaky pastry. When my sister's child was born, I went and stayed with her to hang out, clean laundry, and bake comfort food. When my mom showed up to visit, I had a batch of our Test Kitchen's pumpkin pie bars handy. Upon trying them she declared they were ‘the best pumpkin pie she had ever eaten.’ Since then, they have reigned pumpkin pie supreme and been the most requested dessert on the Dyer family holiday table.”

Cecile Dyer, Senior Video Producer, Baking Education

#9501. Warning Letters Sent to Online Pharmacies Illegally Selling Schedule II Stimulants

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have issued joint warning letters to 2 websites for illegally selling and distributing or dispensing schedule II stimulants, including amphetamine drug products marketed as Adderall.

The warning letters to kubapharm.com and premiumlightsupplier.com state that the websites are selling amphetamine drug products, including Adderall, that are misbranded and in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additionally, by failing to register the online pharmacies with the DEA, despite knowingly or intentionally advertising the sale of controlled substances, these websites are also in violation of the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Act.

“These letters are not only a warning to the companies that illegally sell prescription medications, but they also serve as a warning to consumers who have bought or have considered buying medications online without a legitimate prescription,” said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram. “Consumers cannot trust the safety or legitimacy of pills sold on unaccredited sites.”

In a press release, the Agency reinforced its commitment to stopping online operators illegally selling potentially harmful drug products to consumers. “These particular types of online pharmacies also undermine our efforts to help consumers safely purchase legitimate prescription medicines over the internet,” said FDA Commissioner Robert M. Califf, MD. “FDA will continue partnering with DEA in an effort to safeguard public health and protect consumers who need access to these important medicines.”

FDA and DEA warn online pharmacies illegally selling Adderall to consumers. News release. US Food and Drug Administration. Accessed April 12, 2022. https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/fda-and-dea-warn-online-pharmacies-illegally-selling-adderall-to-consumers-301524032.html

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

The FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

The golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:

A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

There is no single right number, but the median US wedding cost of $10,000 to $15,000 is achievable for most couples without going into debt. Focus on what matters most to you and cut everything else. A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

No. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

Yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Tips for vendors (plan 15-20% for catering staff, bartenders, and drivers), alterations for wedding attire ($200-$500), marriage license fees ($30-$100), and overtime charges if the reception runs past the contracted time. Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.

#9487. The Vitamin Deficiency Linked To Chronic Headaches

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

Blood tests showed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

#9486. Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols

An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”

The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.

Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.

The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.

This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.

This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832

#9484. Pastina Soup (Italian Penicillin)

This soup is my new go-to when my family is sick. The broth here is AMAZING – light, flavorful, and nourishing. Absolute comfort food.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 1, 2026

What an awesome soup recipe! The family loved it! It will be on repeat in our home especially with the kids asking for more!!! Thank you.

Like, slurp that savory broth and go back for a third bowl kind of good.

My daughter got sick last week, which means that our whole family got sick last week. And when I get sick, I lose two things: 1) my appetite, and 2) my interest in cooking.

This pastina soup truly SAVED us last week. It is:

I can’t say enough about how much I loved this last week. I sat down at the table with a steamy bowl with extra parm on top, and found myself repeatedly going back for “just one more scoop” of the broth over those tiny stars, even though I swore I hadn’t been feeling hungry just a moment earlier.

My girls were pretty excited about eating tiny star pasta with olive oil + Parmesan, while Bjork and I ladled the luscious broth over our bowls and finally tucked into some nurturing food for the first time in several days.

Pastina refers to the tiny star shaped pasta, which I found at Target, and the nickname Italian Penicillin refers to the healing nature of the savory broth – almost like a chicken noodle soup, but simpler. (And if I’m being honest, I prefer this to chicken noodle.)

I hope you are healthy and well, physically and emotionally. But if you’re not, this is comfort meal that has been serving our family so well lately!

I keep them real chunky, and I give them a quick sauté with olive oil before adding all the liquid just to get things extra fragrant.

I use water and Better Than Bouillon broth base.

Transfer to a bowl to cool down for a moment.

And then add them right back to the broth pot.

Source Notes: “Italian penicillin” is a nickname for pastina soup, or pastina (small pasta) in broth. It is playfully compared to medicine because of its healing vibe, being that it is a warm, nostalgic, nourishing comfort food. It originated with generations of Italian grandmothers and it has moved into the spotlight after becoming a popular trend on TikTok over the last few years. 🙂

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

Hi, do you know if I can cook the Stelline directly in the broth? Looking forward to trying this recipe! Thank you!

Okay technically yes, I think you could! But here’s why I prefer not to:

– it will make the broth a bit thicker / starchier, and I prefer a silky, light broth

– the noodles will be more at risk of overcooking and getting mushy since they continue to sit in the hot liquid

– it doesn’t keep as well as leftovers (I prefer to just freeze the broth on its own)

– the experience of pouring the broth over the noodles is really fun. 🙂

#9482. Fall Freezer Meals #2

These Fall Freezer Meals have been SO helpful for us. The prep is shockingly easy!

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 14, 2026

A few months ago, I discovered what feels like a little life hack.

I started spending an hour each month getting a few meals prepped for the month ahead. We’re talking just assembling stuff for my favorite recipes into bags and freezing it!

And I can’t tell you how much this system makes me feel like I have my life together! It’s the best.

The recipes this month are absolute family favorites for fall!

And they all have cook times for Crockpot, Instant Pot, and stovetop methods. 🙂

Hope these help make your life easier this month like they have for us!

Everything you need is right on them. I print the cards out and attach them to the bags so I don’t have to use my phone at all for the prep or cooking.

For the streusel: mix 4 tablespoons melted butter, 1/3 cup brown sugar, and 3/4 cup flour into small crumbles.

Spray a muffin tin with avocado oil. Fill tins two-thirds of the way full with batter; top with streusel.

Store muffins in an airtight container or bag in the freezer (or fridge). To reheat from frozen, microwave 45-60 seconds.

Remove chicken from the sauce and shred. Blend sauce until smooth. Add chicken back in. Serve in tortillas with all the taco fixings you want!

Add 1-2 cups heavy cream and 1-2 cups chicken broth (as needed). To thicken: whisk 2 tbsp. cornstarch with 2 tbsp. cold water; add and simmer.

Whisk 1 1/2 tbsp. cornstarch in 1 1/2 tbsp. cold water; add to bubbling pot and let simmer until slightly thickened.

Stir in 2 cups of fresh spinach and fresh cilantro just before serving.

Serve with rice and chili crisp. I also love this with cucumber salad (thinly sliced cucumber and red onion, tossed with vinegar, avocado oil, salt, and sugar).

#9481. Sloppy Joe’s with Ranch Potatoes

Easy, saucy, delicious Sloppy Joe’s! My kids’ favorite dinner. Super simple to make with just a few ingredients.

Published by Lindsay Ostrom on October 28, 2026

Here’s the thing – it’s humble, it’s non-fancy, but my husband and my kids are so happy when I make this for dinner.

I’ve been on a JOURNEY with these. I tried making Sloppy Joe’s several ways this summer, since my daughter kept asking for them. But with every batch I made, she always kindly let me know that they were still “not as good as the ones at school.”

Lucky for me (and all of us), I know several of the wonderful people who do the food service at their school. I was able to get some school recipe intel, which is how I ended up with this very simple “recipe”:

It’s rich, and meaty, and easy, and just so very family-friendly.

Bjork and I like ours topped with pickled jalapenos or crispy onions, and the girls, of course, like them “plain” on a squishy white bun.

I always always make these with what we call Ranch Potatoes, which are the truly the delight of my life. In our house, it’s not Sloppy Joe’s if there’s no pile of crispy, buttery Ranch Potatoes on the side. 🙂

Regarding diced onion, pepper, or garlic in the Sloppy Joe filling: this recipe has none. Everyone I cook for enjoys these the same (or even more?) with an uncluttered texture and just a few hits of garlic and onion powder instead, which makes this whole thing even faster and easier.

My youngest requested this as her birthday meal this year. Hope you like it as much as we do!

Leave it sitting undisturbed for a few minutes so that it develops a nice golden crust.

Garlic powder, onion powder, beef bouillon, ketchup, and BBQ sauce!

Add some water as needed to make the mixture loosen up and turn a bit glossy. It can just hang out until you’re ready to eat.

When you’re close to eating, pop your potatoes in the oven.

Once they’re roasty toasty, add a knob of butter and some ranch seasoning. Toss to combine. (If you don’t have ranch seasoning, just use melted butter, fresh garlic, and dill. UNREAL.)

Load it onto a soft bun – we love this with ranch potatoes and green beans!

5 Stars 4 Stars 3 Stars 2 Stars 1 Star

Easy, saucy, delicious Sloppy Joe’s! My kids’ favorite dinner. We love these with Ranch Potatoes!

White garlic sauce (for dipping, as shown in the video): Whisk 1/4 cup mayo, 1/4 cup plain Greek yogurt, 1 clove grated garlic, 1-2 tablespoons water, and salt to taste.

Making Ahead: The meat mixture is ready to go right after you add the ketchup and BBQ sauce, but I usually like to let it simmer for 30-60 minutes to really caramelize around the edges and deepen in both flavor and color. It also works perfectly to keep it warm in the crockpot after cooking!

#9480. Increased Risk for Suicide Attempts Among Children Who Use Tobacco Products

Children who report the use of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes and vaping — have a 3 to 5 times increased risk for suicide attempts (SAs), according to study results published in JAMA Network Open.

New tobacco products (ie, e-cigarettes, vapes, hookahs) have become increasingly popular in the United States, particularly among children and adolescents. Although it is well-documented that adolescents and adults who smoke cigarettes have an increased likelihood of suicidality, it is unclear whether this heightened risk applies to children who use tobacco products.

To address this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a cross-sectional cohort study from September 1 to September 5, 2022. The researchers used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a nationally representative cohort of 11,868 US children enrolled at 9 and 10 years of age. The objective of the current study was to investigate the correlation between tobacco product use and the incidence of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation (SI), and SAs among preadolescent children. Substance use was evaluated using the ABCD Youth Substance Use Interview and hair toxicology tests at baseline, a 6-month follow-up, and then yearly. The researchers assessed suicidality using children and caregiver reports of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS-5).

The researchers included data from 8988 children (median age, 9.8 years; 47.9% girls). At baseline, 1.1% of children reported ever using tobacco products, and this prevalence rose significantly to 1.7% at the 18-month follow-up. The researchers observed no statistical difference in smoking experience by sex or race/ethnicity; however, tobacco-using children generally came from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, had greater prenatal smoking exposure, and were more likely to have parents with a history of depression, alcohol issues, and behavioral or suicide-related problems, relative to children who did not use tobacco products.

The researchers observed significant associations between tobacco product use among children and increased risks for SAs at each time point. Tobacco use was linked to a 3 to 5 times higher risk for SAs, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.67 (95% CI, 2.35-9.27; P <.001) at baseline, 4.25 (95% CI, 2.33-7.74; P <.001) at 1 year, and 2.85 (95% CI, 1.58-5.12; P =.001) at year 2.

The researchers also evaluated whether children’s personality, cognition, and psychological outcomes were associated with tobacco product use. They found that children were more likely to endorse tobacco use if they had conduct disorder (P <.001), oppositional defiant disorder (P <.001), rule-breaking behaviors (P <.001), aggressive behaviors (P <.001), social problems (P =.009), attention problems (P =.02), as well as personality traits of lack of planning (P <.001), positive urgency (P =.006), lack of perseverance (P =.009), sensation seeking (P =.02), aggression (P =.02), negative urgency (P =.03), and depressive mood (P <.05).

However, the association between tobacco use and SAs remained elevated, independent of these behavioral/psychopathology traits (OR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.70-5.65; P <.001) in regression analyses. Conversely, the association between tobacco use and SI was not sustained when childhood behavioral measures were considered.

Among other substance use, only alcohol sipping was independently associated with SAs (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.13; P =.007). These findings suggest that while other substance use is related to SAs, tobacco product use remains a robust independent risk factor.

Study authors concluded, “The findings suggest that smoking tobacco products may be a modifiable risk factor that can be addressed in suicide prevention efforts, especially among children.”

These study findings may be limited by the use of hair toxicology tests to assess tobacco use and the inability to determine causality, given the observational study design.

Lee PH, Tervo-Clemmens B, Liu RT, et al. Use of tobacco products and suicide attempts among elementary school-aged children. JAMA Netw Open. Published online February 5, 2024. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.0376

#9479. The Simple Drink Swap Linked To 41% More Weight Loss

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, said:

“It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($25,500 in 2027), HSA ($4,500 individual / $9,000 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $25,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

If you are 40 with $50,000 saved and feeling behind, shifting from a 10% savings rate to a 40% savings rate on a $100,000 income adds $30,000 per year to your investment accounts. At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

Most employers allow you to change your 401(k) contribution rate at any time. Increasing by 2% of salary is small enough that you will barely notice the paycheck reduction, but it compounds dramatically over time. Repeat this increase every six months until you are maxing out your 401(k).

Roughly one in four employees leaves free employer match money on the table. If your employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary, you need to contribute at least 6% to capture the full match. This is an instant 50% return on your money — no investment can beat it.

A Roth IRA provides tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, with no required minimum distributions. The 2026 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+). If your income exceeds the Roth limits, use the backdoor Roth conversion strategy to contribute indirectly.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The national median for under-35 is only $13,000, so if you have more than that, you are already ahead of most peers.

The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

Generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

It is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $75,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

#9474. Easy Eggplant Bolognese (1 Pot!)

Disclosure: This post may contain affiliate links which provide us a small commission when used for purchase. We're grateful for your support!

When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

Even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

Bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

Our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

This 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

Build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

Once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

When it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

We think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!

It’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).

If you try this recipe, let us know! Leave a comment, rate it, and don’t forget to tag a photo @minimalistbaker on Instagram. Cheers, friends!

#9473. Spike in ADHD, Autism Diagnoses Driven by Broader Recognition, Understanding

Two new studies suggest autism and ADHD are becoming better recognized, not actually more prevalent, and that executive function and social challenges seen in both conditions actually stem from different underlying brain mechanisms.

ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) share overlapping symptoms, and prior studies suggest that nearly half of autistic children also have ADHD.1 Now, two new studies on ADHD and ASD profiles suggest that rising diagnosis rates are a product of improved symptom recognition and diagnostic practices, and that executive function and social impairments seen in both ADHD and ASD may be traced to different cognitive pathways.

The first study, published in JAMA Psychiatry,2 evaluated the health records of 71,000 children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and 713,000 controls; it found that the annual number of individuals in the nationwide Danish health registry with newly diagnosed ADHD and/or ASD increased from 4,944 in 2012 to 9,179 in 2022. The proportion of girls diagnosed with ADHD or ASD and the median age at diagnosis also grew during the 10-year study period from 2012 to 2022.

However, traditional risk factors strongly linked to an ADHD or ASD diagnosis in 2012, such as low birth weight or lower household income, have become progressively less predictive with time. For example, children born with a low birth weight were 54% more likely to receive a subsequent diagnosis of ADHD or ASD in 2012; by 2022, that percentage dropped to 17%. Overall, the study found that children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD or ASD today more closely resemble their neurotypical peers compared to those diagnosed 10 years ago.

These findings do not mean that ADHD or ASD has become less impairing; the spectrum of cases has shifted as clinicians get better at identifying less obvious cases. Greater awareness of ADHD and ASD, and broader access to diagnostic assessment tools, are also factors contributing to growing diagnoses among children.

“The study results do not show that these conditions are being overdiagnosed, or that they have become less severe,” says Oleguer Plana-Ripoll, Ph.D., a senior author of the study. “Rather, they indicate that the population receiving these diagnoses has changed over time, and this needs to be taken into account when interpreting current trends.”

The second, smaller study, published in Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry,3 found that executive functioning (EF) and social cognition (SC) impairments in children diagnosed with ADHD or ASD may look similar, but the impairments stem from different underlying mechanisms.

The cross-sectional, four-year study analyzed performance-based measures of 123 children, aged 6 to 11 years, across three matched groups: mild ASD, combined-type ADHD, and neurotypical peers.

Findings indicated that both ADHD and ASD groups performed worse than their neurotypical peers on measures of EF and SC. However, children with ADHD demonstrated weak social cognition due to difficulties with response inhibition and attention. Social cognition weaknesses in children with ASD, on the other hand, appeared to result from difficulties in understanding and interpreting social information.

More specifically, children in the ASD group performed significantly worse than children with ADHD on measures of:

Children with ASD also displayed more difficulties than did children with ADHD on executive function tasks that measured the ability to shift between rules and adapt strategies.

Children in the ADHD group performed significantly worse than those in the ASD group on measures of:

How executive functions related to social cognition across disorders was the strongest indication of different cognitive processes between the two clinical groups. In the ADHD group, the theory-of-mind model explained 72% of the variance, compared to just 55% in the ASD group.

The researchers surmise that a person with ADHD relies heavily on executive functions, such as inhibition, auditory attention, and design fluency, for social cognition. In essence, their difficulties in social situations are not because they don’t understand social concepts but because distractions and impulsivity interfere.

In the ASD group, social difficulties were more likely to stem from affect recognition (understanding facial cues) and response set (cognitive flexibility, shifting perspectives), rather than from attention deficit or impulse control.

“ADHD and autism are two separate and distinct conditions that happen to be found together much more frequently than would be expected by chance alone,” says ADHD expert William Dodson, M.D., LF-APA. “For people with co-existing ADHD and ASD, treating the ADHD is a means to an end. The world is a classroom for people with ASD, and they have to be ready to observe and practice what they’ve learned.”

Results from the study suggest individuals would benefit more from targeted ADHD and ASD interventions matched to each disorder-specific profile rather than a single shared approach.

1Lydia Furman, MD, Children with Both Autism Spectrum Disorder and Attention Deficit Disorder- New Insights (March, 2018). publications.aap.org/journal-blogs/blog/pdfDownload/2377

2Tarp, M.E., Lousdal, M.L., Rask, C.U., et al. (2026). Changes in characteristics associated with ADHD and ASD diagnoses over time. JAMA Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.2722

3Pastorino, G.M.G., Olivieri, M., Aquino, A., Mungo, N., Suriano, R., and Operto, F.F. (2026) Neurocognitive endophenotypes in neurodevelopmental disorders: social cognition and executive functions in children with autism spectrum disorder level 1 and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Front. Child Adolesc. Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.3389/frcha.2026.1920753

#9472. Physician Burnout by Specialty & Other Physician Mental Health Statistics

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, physicians continue to experience burnout at alarmingly high rates. In a recent survey of 2440 physicians, approximately 63% of respondents reported having at least 1 manifestation of burnout in 2021; this was higher than all 4 prior assessment time points since 2011.1 Because physician burnout is more common in certain specialties, it is crucial to identify trends and offer help to those at higher risk. This article examines the symptoms, causes, and prevalence of burnout among clinicians in various specialties, and outlines strategies physicians can use to address burnout.

The American Medical Association (AMA) defines physician burnout as a long-term stress reaction that can include the following2:

For many clinicians, symptoms of burnout were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, chronic stress due to work overload, exposure to infected patients, lack of protective equipment, and poor efforts to control infection rates increased the risk of burnout.3 Other factors associated with burnout include system inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and increased regulation and technology requirements.2

The consequences of physician burnout affect patients as well as clinicians. From a patient’s perspective, physician burnout can result in poor physician/patient rapport, adherence to treatment, and treatment outcomes.4 For physicians, burnout can lead to declining mental health and subsequent depression, substance abuse, and suicide.4

Although burnout affects clinicians in all specialties and practice settings, the rate is higher in certain specialties. The AMA’s Organization Biopsy® is an assessment tool large health care organizations can use to measure and improve the health of their organizations.5 One of the parameters this tool measures is burnout.

The AMA’s 2022 Organizational Biopsy received more than 13,000 responses from physicians and other clinicians from more than 70 organizations in 30 states. The specialties with the highest rates of burnout were as follows6:

Medscape conducts an annual survey on physician lifestyle and happiness that includes questions about burnout and depression. In 2023, this 10-minute online survey included input from 9,175 physicians in 29 specialties.7 Overall for all specialties, 36% of respondents said they felt burned out, 5% said they felt depressed, and 18% said they felt both burned out and depressed.8 Based on the Medscape 2023 survey results, the following sections summarize the rates of burnout and depression among physicians clinicians working in emergency medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology, and internal medicine.

In Medscape’s 2023 survey, emergency physicians reported the following8:

Burnout was reported by a higher proportion of women (51%) than men (38%). The 3 largest factors contributing to burnout among emergency medicine physicians were having too many bureaucratic tasks (51%), a lack of respect from patients (50%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (46%).8

Slightly more than one-half of female family physicians (51%) and one-third of male family physicians (33%) reported experiencing burnout.9 The overall proportion of respondents who said they felt burned out was 42%. Depression affected 4% of family medicine physicians, while 15% said they felt both burned out and depressed.9

By far the largest contributor to family physician burnout was having too many bureaucratic tasks; 73% of respondents reported tasks such as paperwork and charting were the main culprit. Working too many hours and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff were cited as factors contributing to burnout by 36% and 31% of respondents, respectively.9

Overall, 39% of pediatricians reported feeling burned out.11 More female pediatricians reported feeling burned out more than their male counterparts (46% vs 26%, respectively).10 The proportion of respondents who said they felt depressed was 3%, while 19% reported being both burned out and depressed.

The 3 largest contributors to burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (65%), lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (40%), and spending too many hours at work (38%).10

In Medscape’s 2023 report, obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported the following11:

Obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported that the 3 largest contributors to their burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (56%), spending too many hours at work (47%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (42%).11

Nearly half of female internists (49%) reported dealing with burnout, vs 31% of male internists.12 However, 4% of both male and female internists said they felt depressed, and 21% of both male and female internists said they felt both burned out and depressed.12

Having too many bureaucratic tasks was the primary contributor to internist burnout (64%). Insufficient compensation/salary was the second-leading factor (40%), followed by a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (35%).12

Many of the factors known to contribute to burnout are systemic and need to be addressed by health care organizations.2 However, physicians can take action to limit their stress and prevent exhaustion. The following strategies may help mitigate burnout2,4,13:

#9470. When Your Body’s Operating System Glitches

The autonomic nervous system regulates everything from heart rate to digestion. Abnormalities may contribute to ADHD and POTS symptoms.

You probably don’t give much thought to how your heart speeds up during exercise or how blood continues flowing to your brain when you stand up. These essential functions are managed by the autonomic nervous system, the body’s complex operating system, which runs quietly in the background.

The autonomic nervous system controls heart rate, blood pressure, the digestive process, body temperature, and continuous blood circulation in the presence of gravity — squeezing blood out of the legs and torso and redistributing it to the head and heart when you move from lying down or sitting to standing.

Some studies suggest that autonomic nervous system abnormalities may contribute to ADHD symptoms like inattention and impulsiveness. Clinicians may notice and use these symptoms to diagnose ADHD, but the underlying cause might reflect atypical autonomic nervous system activity.

Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) is an atypical or malfunctioning state of the autonomic nervous system. People with ADHD and/or hypermobility appear to have a higher prevalence of POTS than do members of the general population. Symptoms include dizziness or fainting when standing up from a sitting or lying position due to sudden changes in blood pressure and heart rate.

[Read: ADHD’s Curious Connections to Chronic Inflammation and Dysautonomia]

In individuals with hypermobility, autonomic dysregulation may be caused by irritation of the nerves that are intermittently stretched due to lax ligaments at the craniocervical junction, where the brain and upper spine meet.

A tilt table test, which measures your heart rate and blood pressure as you change position, is the main way POTS is diagnosed. Other assessments include blood and urine tests and a measure of the autonomic nerves that control sweating.

[Read: Exploring the ADHD-Inflammation Link]

Arthur L. Jenkins, III, M.D., FACS, FAANS, is a board-certified neurosurgeon and founder of Jenkins NeuroSpine in New York and Connecticut.
